page_placements.theme: Transfer, adaptation and retention depend on source alignment and recipe

record.tranche_reason: The study develops and tests scaling laws for repeated domain data, finding that test loss can rise from overfitting and is better represented by a sum of power-law terms than by one power law. It also tests extrapolation of its own fitted laws.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own domain-loss scaling and extrapolation results for specialized pretraining. It does not run a conventional sweep of held-out general-language pretraining loss across parameters, tokens, and compute, or compare the Kaplan and Hoffmann compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Cited results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study fits its own scaling laws for held-out domain test loss under heavy repetition of a small domain set during pretraining. It argues a single power law cannot capture the overfitting stage and proposes a sum of two power laws. It also tests forecasts from these fits. Together this bears on V5 (repeated data, fine-tuning), V7 (bending away from one power law; exponents depend on data mix) and V2 (extrapolation, though only about 2× in tokens and across mixture fractions). The SPT-vs-NPT comparisons (r1–r13, r23–r25) are method-benefit results, not scaling-law tests.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that domain data should be mixed into pretraining as early as possible, because SPT improves domain loss, reduces forgetting and can let a 1B model beat a 3B NPT model. The best mixture depends on domain-set size and training budget. Their sum-of-two-power-laws overfitting law, fitted on pilot runs, forecasts domain loss and the best mixture.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines specialized domain-data mixing and repeated-data overfitting, rather than reproducing the original scaling-law experiments or their parameter/token/compute allocation analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The best domain-mixture fraction changes with pretraining horizon; it also depends on domain dataset size. For 3M–30M-token subsets, gains can diminish or become negative at longer horizons, while 300M-token MusicPile maintains gains. The fitted model parameterizes exponents and coefficients by mixture fraction.

fits_no_version.finding: SPT lowers post-finetuning domain loss by 0.8–2.0%, cuts the tokens needed by 1.40–1.75×, and a 1B SPT model can close 23–133% of the 1B-to-3B NPT gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Mixing scarce domain data into pretraining is more token- and parameter-efficient than reserving it for finetuning.

fits_no_version.finding: The loss-minimizing domain mixture fraction shrinks as the training horizon grows: 10% best under 30B tokens, 2–5% at 200B, 2% past 240B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal repetition fraction of a fixed domain set is compute-dependent.

fits_no_version.finding: For small domain sets (3M–30M tokens), SPT gains vanish or reverse at long horizons. Late introduction (SCPT) helps at 30M tokens but not at 3M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The best timing of domain-data exposure depends on dataset size and repetition.

fits_no_version.finding: SPT improves downstream MCQA accuracy over NPT after finetuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain data in pretraining improves downstream domain accuracy after finetuning.

record.problems: The results use a controlled OLMo-based training environment and are focused on specialized domain data rather than general-purpose language-model scaling. Several curve comparisons are described qualitatively or shown in figures without exact values in the text. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: The study reports additional plotted comparisons and loss trajectories across models, mixtures, and budgets, but not enough separately stated numeric outcomes in the text to record them as distinct rows. The general Dolma-loss comparison during SPT is described as comparable up to 5% mixture and degraded at 10% in Appendix F, but does not test a listed claim version. Related-work findings cited from other studies were excluded.

untested.parts: Entirely untested. All loss-scaling results are in a data-bottlenecked, repeated-data regime at fixed model size. There is no sweep of parameters, tokens or compute in the non-bottleneck regime.
Extrapolation to runs orders of magnitude larger in compute or parameters. The forecasts span only about 2× in tokens, or cross mixture fractions.
Entirely untested. Depth is varied to make the 3B model, but there is no comparison at fixed parameter count.
Image, video and other modalities; transfer scaling across model sizes.
Entirely untested. Downstream accuracy is compared between pipelines only.

missing.what: The change in domain test loss after finetuning (ΔTest) follows a power law in pretraining tokens, ΔTest = aT^b + c, on all three domains. This bears on V5 (fine-tuning regime).
The fitted gap exponent b_gap is positive but stays below 1 for all mixtures up to 10%, so overfitting grows sublinearly. This bears on the fitted exponents.
Post-finetuning domain test loss falls with model size (300M–3B) for both NPT and SPT, but no power-law fit is reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links to V1 were removed. Repeated domain data is a data-bottlenecked regime, and no sweep over parameters or compute is fitted. V2 is supported only narrowly: the extrapolation is about 2× in tokens and across δ, not orders of magnitude. Rows r1–r13 are method comparisons, not scaling-law results. ChemPile and ProofPile fit quality appears only in figures, with no fit metrics reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test the conventional non-bottleneck regime across parameters, tokens, and compute; its loss-scaling evidence concerns domain data repeated during specialized pretraining, with model size generally fixed.
Tests extrapolations for specialized-pretraining domain loss, not predictions of general held-out pretraining loss across orders of magnitude in model size or compute.
Does not find the loss-minimizing parameter-count and token-count allocation for a fixed compute budget.
Does not compare depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.

Tests repeated domain data in language-model training and domain corpora including symbolic music, chemistry, and proofs. It does not test image or video models, and does not establish one power law for every modality or training regime.
Reports downstream-task differences between training pipelines, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.

Does not compare published Kaplan and Hoffmann allocation exponents or systematically vary parameter counting, architecture, or fitting methods. Its fit-dependence evidence concerns repeated-domain-data loss curves and mixture fraction.
